speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To understand your episodes of dizziness and vertigo, please describe exactly what you feel and how long each episode lasts. Also, have you noticed any accompanying symptoms like hearing loss, nausea, or visual changes?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. The fact that your dizziness is position-dependent strongly suggests a peripheral cause. Is there any associated tinnitus, ear fullness, or a history of sudden hearing loss on the affected side? Also, do you experience any new onset headache, double vision, or difficulty speaking during these spells?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
You mentioned a doctor previously suspected migraines, but your symptoms are strictly position-dependent without headache, nausea, or hearing changes. Given your age and the specific nature of these episodes, I need to rule out a central cause or other vestibular issues.

REQUEST TEST: Audiometry to confirm baseline hearing status and assess for vestibular hyperacusis.
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI of the brain focusing on the posterior fossa and cerebellum.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The combination of age, purely position-dependent vertigo, absence of auditory symptoms, and lack of central neurological signs makes BPPV the most likely diagnosis despite the previous suggestion of migraine.
